title: The Chelyabinsk Meteor: 30 Hiroshima Bombs From a 20 m Rock
description:
Unreal but true: a new real event every day at 5:48 pm (Riyadh).

On the morning of February 15, 2013, a rock about 20 meters wide (NASA: about 17 to 20 m) entered the sky over Chelyabinsk, Russia, and exploded about 30 km up. For a moment the fireball was brighter than the Sun. It released about 400 to 500 kilotons of energy (NASA's later estimate: 440 kilotons), roughly 30 times the atomic bomb dropped on Hiroshima. The blast wave blew in windows across the region: about 1,500 people (1,491 by one count) needed medical treatment, mostly for cuts from broken glass. No deaths were reported.

The scene is drawn side-on with a made-up skyline; heights, the path angle and timing are not to scale or real time. The bomb counter shows the total energy; in reality almost all of it was released in the last seconds as the rock broke up.

Sources: NASA JPL, "Additional Details on the Large Feb. 15 Fireball over Russia" (17 to 20 m, 440 kilotons, brighter than the Sun); The Planetary Society, "What was the Chelyabinsk meteor event?" (about 20 m, about 30 times Hiroshima, about 30 km up, about 1,500 hurt by flying glass); Catalina Sky Survey / University of Arizona, "How big was the 2013 Chelyabinsk asteroid?" (about 20 m, about 30 times Hiroshima, brighter than the Sun); Space.com, "Chelyabinsk Meteor: A Wake-Up Call for Earth"; Wikipedia, "Chelyabinsk meteor" (400 to 500 kilotons, 1,491 injured mainly by glass, no deaths).
Animation drawn in code; narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs).

Did you guess it? Tell me your number in the comments.
